analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicare's drug price negotiation: more drugs, sooner, deeper discounts.
analysis.headline: The SMART Prices Act, a Medicare drug price bill backed by 27 senators, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill strengthens the Medicare drug price negotiation program created in the Inflation Reduction Act. It would raise the number of drugs Medicare negotiates prices for each year from 15 to 50, cut the years a drug is shielded from negotiation from 7 to 3 for small-molecule drugs and from 11 to 3 for biologics, and set larger minimum discounts off manufacturers' list prices, starting with prices that take effect in 2028. Lower negotiated prices reduce out-of-pocket drug costs for the tens of millions of people on Medicare and reduce federal drug spending.
analysis.who_benefits: People on Medicare, roughly 65 million Americans, who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs, plus taxpayers who help fund Medicare's drug benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the number of drugs Medicare negotiates each year from 15 to 50, so far more brand-name drugs eventually fall under negotiated prices.
Shortens the waiting period before a drug becomes negotiable from 7 years to 3 for small-molecule drugs and from 11 years to 3 for biologics, meaning newer drugs reach negotiated prices much sooner.
Deepens the minimum negotiated discounts off manufacturers' prices, from 75% to 76%, 65% to 55%, and 40% to 30% depending on the drug's age and type.
Applies the stronger terms to Medicare prices beginning with initial price applicability year 2028.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare revenues and margins on selected drugs shrink under deeper discounts and earlier negotiation.

drawbacks.text: Shortening the negotiation window from 7-11 years to 3 years cuts into the exclusivity period that brand-name drug makers use to recoup research costs; the industry argues this reduces incentives to develop new medicines, and an honest supporter of lower prices has to weigh that risk.

The bill covers only the Medicare program's negotiation program; it does not directly address prices in employer insurance or the individual market, so many working-age Americans see no immediate change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the gains are concrete: more drugs negotiated, sooner, at bigger discounts, paid for by manufacturers rather than by patients or taxpayers. The main cost is the industry's argument that shorter exclusivity could slow future drug development; the bill also does nothing directly for people under 65, so its benefits are concentrated among seniors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has taken place.

narrative.text: Sen. Klobuchar introduced the SMART Prices Act on May 21, 2025, with 26 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, including Sens. Welch, Warren, and Booker.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the action history shows no further action since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who avoid the deeper discounts and earlier negotiation the bill would impose, and the status quo more broadly.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strengthen the Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare drug price negotiation program.

for.name: 26 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Democrats and one independent, including Welch, Warren, Booker, and Durbin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none from the Republican side.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in the Finance Committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill cuts their Medicare revenues directly: 50 drugs negotiated instead of 15 each year, exclusivity cut to 3 years, and minimum discounts deepened to as much as 76% off list prices. Their interest in blocking it runs against beneficiaries' interest in cheaper drugs.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical industry trade groups and lobbying (e.g., PhRMA)
industries.note: Stronger Medicare negotiation is the industry's most costly policy exposure; they lobby to preserve the current, weaker program rather than the expanded one this bill would create.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsor and no committee action more than a year after introduction, the bill is likely to die in the Senate Finance Committee. Passing would require a markup that Finance has not scheduled, then 60 votes to advance on the Senate floor, a high bar without Republican support, unless drug pricing is attached to a larger must-pass bill.
